title: Landmark Ruling: ICJ Declares Right to Strike Protected Under 1948 Labor Treaty
summary: In a historic decision, the United Nations’ highest court affirmed on Thursday that the right to strike is enshrined in a foundational labor treaty—even though the word “strike” never appears in its text. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) was asked by the International Labor Organization (ILO) to settle a long-running dispute over whether the 1948 Freedom of Association and Protection of the Right to Organize Convention implicitly guarantees workers the ability to walk off the job. The 14-judge panel unanimously agreed that it does. “The protection of the right to strike is encompassed in the freedom of association,” ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa declared from the Great Hall of Justice in The Hague. The advisory opinion is not legally binding, but it carries significant moral and political authority, potentially influencing labor regulations, international trade agreements, and court rulings worldwide. The convention has been ratified by 158 countries and is embedded in standards set by the UN, the OECD, and various trade pacts. Notably, the United States—an ILO member—has not ratified the convention. Labor unions celebrated the ruling as a crucial victory. “As any trade unionist will tell you, there is no right to organize without the right to strike!” said Christy Hoffman, general-secretary of UNI Global Union. International labor law expert Paul van der Heijden told the Associated Press that the opinion gives workers a vital tool when their actions face legal challenges. However, the court carefully noted that the right is not absolute. The opinion “does not entail any determination on the precise content, scope or conditions for the exercise of that right,” Iwasawa said, acknowledging that restrictions may apply in essential services. The ILO sought the opinion in 2023 after internal disagreements. During hearings last October, 18 countries and five organizations presented arguments, with a majority supporting the right to strike—already recognized in most European nations. The decision adds to the ICJ’s recent influential advisory opinions, including a 2025 ruling on climate change obligations.
why_it_matters: This ruling empowers workers around the world by confirming that a core labor treaty protects their ability to strike, even when the law is silent. For students who will one day have jobs, it underlines how international law can safeguard basic rights and influence national policies.

background_read: The International Court of Justice (ICJ), seated in The Hague, Netherlands, is the United Nations' principal judicial organ and settles disputes between states, but also gives advisory opinions on legal questions posed by UN agencies.

The International Labor Organization (ILO), founded in 1919 after World War I, is a UN specialized agency that brings together governments, employers, and workers to set international labor standards.
Its 1948 Freedom of Association and Protection of the Right to Organize Convention (No. 87) is one of eight fundamental ILO conventions, guaranteeing workers the right to form and join unions.

For decades, an internal dispute simmered over whether the convention implicitly includes the right to strike; while many European nations and courts recognized it, some employers and governments argued it was not explicitly written.

The ICJ's unanimous advisory opinion settles that debate by interpreting the treaty's principles broadly, joining a line of recent influential opinions—such as the 2025 ruling on state obligations to fight climate change—that shape international norms even when not legally binding.

perspectives.description: Labor unions and workers gain a powerful legal precedent to challenge government or employer restrictions on strikes, potentially leading to stronger collective bargaining and fairer conditions worldwide.

Opponents worry that an undefined right to strike could be abused, disrupting essential services like healthcare or transportation, and might lead to calls for stricter legislation that actually limits workers' actions.

The opinion demonstrates how international courts can fill treaty gaps through interpretation, raising deep questions about democratic legitimacy and the balance between written text and evolving intent in international law.

The ruling may encourage more ILO complaints and influence trade negotiations; countries that restrict strikes could face increased pressure to reform, while the U.S. might now face renewed debate on ratifying the convention.
